u4.intro: A periodic table and the AP Chemistry equations sheet are allowed, and a calculator may be used throughout.

mc.stem:
Questions 1-4 refer to the following.

A student is asked to find the mass percent of Na₂CO₃ in a white powder that is a mixture of Na₂CO₃ and NaCl only. She dissolves 2.500 g of the powder in about 50 mL of distilled water and adds 40.0 mL of 0.500 M CaCl₂(aq); a white precipitate of CaCO₃ forms. She collects the solid on a filter paper of mass 0.912 g, rinses it with distilled water, and then dries, cools and weighs it three times.
Weighing · mass of filter paper + solid (g)
After 1st drying · 2.614
After 2nd drying · 2.431
After 3rd drying · 2.429
Molar masses (g/mol): Na₂CO₃ 105.99, NaCl 58.44, CaCO₃ 100.09. All sodium salts are soluble in water; CaCO₃ is insoluble.

parts.q:
Which of the following is closest to the mass percent of Na₂CO₃ in the powder?
(A) 60.7%
(B) 64.3%
(C) 72.1%
(D) 84.8%
parts.a: (B). The mass must be read once the solid is dry: the 2nd and 3rd weighings agree (2.431 g and 2.429 g), so m(CaCO₃) = 2.429 − 0.912 = 1.517 g. n(CaCO₃) = 1.517 g ÷ 100.09 g/mol = 1.516 × 10⁻² mol, and each CO₃²⁻ came from one Na₂CO₃, so m(Na₂CO₃) = 1.516 × 10⁻² mol × 105.99 g/mol = 1.606 g, which is 1.606 ÷ 2.500 = 64.3% of the powder. (A) divides the mass of CaCO₃ by the sample mass, as if the precipitate were the Na₂CO₃ itself; the two compounds have different molar masses. (C) uses the first weighing, 1.702 g of solid, which still held water that the later dryings removed. (D) assumes that all 2.00 × 10⁻² mol of the added Ca²⁺ precipitated, but Ca²⁺ was in excess, so the carbonate, not the Ca²⁺, sets the mass of precipitate.
parts.n: 4.5.A.1 and 4.5.A.2 (topic 4.5), skill 5.F. Thinking: turn a constant-mass weighing into moles of precipitate, then go back through the 1:1 ratio to the analyte. Trap: (C), using the first weighing before the solid had reached constant mass.

parts.q:
Her lab partner proposes adding only 10.0 mL of the 0.500 M CaCl₂(aq) instead of 40.0 mL, to save reagent. Which of the following best evaluates the proposal?
(A) Acceptable, because a precipitation goes to completion, so even a small amount of CaCl₂ converts all of the carbonate to CaCO₃.
(B) Not acceptable, because unreacted Na₂CO₃ would be trapped in the solid, so the calculated percent would come out too high.
(C) Acceptable, because Ca²⁺ is a spectator ion, so the amount of CaCl₂ added does not change the mass of precipitate that forms.
(D) Not acceptable, because 10.0 mL supplies only 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol Ca²⁺, so the calculated percent would be about 21%, far too low.
parts.a: (D). 10.0 mL × 0.500 M = 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol Ca²⁺, but the sample holds 1.52 × 10⁻² mol CO₃²⁻. Ca²⁺ would become the limiting reactant, only 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol CaCO₃ could form, and the student would calculate 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol × 105.99 g/mol ÷ 2.500 g = 21.2% instead of 64.3%. A gravimetric analysis works only when the precipitating reagent is in excess, as the original 40.0 mL (2.00 × 10⁻² mol Ca²⁺) is. (A) confuses a reaction going to completion with every reactant being used up: the reaction stops when the limiting reactant runs out. (B) gets the direction wrong: leftover carbonate stays dissolved and passes into the filtrate, so the precipitate is too small, not too large. (C) misidentifies the spectators: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectators, while Ca²⁺ is part of the precipitate.
parts.n: 4.5.A.2 (topic 4.5), skill 2.F. Thinking: before trusting a gravimetric result, compare moles to check that the precipitating reagent is in excess. Trap: (A), which reads 'goes to completion' as 'uses up all of the analyte'.

parts.q:
Which test on a portion of the filtrate would confirm that enough CaCl₂ was added in the original procedure to precipitate all of the carbonate?
(A) Test the electrical conductivity of the filtrate; if it conducts, excess Ca²⁺ ions must still be dissolved in it.
(B) Evaporate the filtrate to dryness; if a white solid remains, all of the Na₂CO₃ was converted into CaCO₃.
(C) Add a few drops of Na₂CO₃(aq); if a white precipitate forms, Ca²⁺ is left over, so no carbonate remained.
(D) Check that the filtrate is clear and colorless; if no cloudiness appears, no carbonate is left in solution.
parts.a: (C). If adding more carbonate produces more CaCO₃, the filtrate still contains Ca²⁺, so Ca²⁺ was the excess reactant and CO₃²⁻ the limiting one: essentially every carbonate ion from the sample has been precipitated. (A) fails because the filtrate conducts whatever the outcome: it always contains Na⁺ and Cl⁻ from the sample and from the CaCl₂. (B) fails for the same reason: NaCl is left when the filtrate evaporates, whether or not any carbonate remained. (D) fails because dissolved Na₂CO₃ is itself clear and colorless, so a clear filtrate says nothing about whether carbonate ions remain.
parts.n: 4.7.A.5 (topic 4.7), skill 2.C. Thinking: a useful test gives different results depending on whether the reagent was in excess; a test that always gives the same result proves nothing. Trap: (D), reading 'clear' as 'no carbonate'.

parts.q:
Which of the following ranks the dissolved ions in the filtrate from the greatest to the least number of moles?
(A) Cl⁻ > Na⁺ > Ca²⁺, with essentially no CO₃²⁻
(B) Na⁺ > Cl⁻ > Ca²⁺, with essentially no CO₃²⁻
(C) Na⁺ > Cl⁻ > CO₃²⁻, with essentially no Ca²⁺
(D) Cl⁻ > Na⁺, with essentially no Ca²⁺ or CO₃²⁻
parts.a: (A). The sample holds 1.606 g Na₂CO₃ (1.516 × 10⁻² mol) and 2.500 − 1.606 = 0.894 g NaCl (1.53 × 10⁻² mol). Na⁺ = 2(1.516 × 10⁻²) + 1.53 × 10⁻² = 4.56 × 10⁻² mol. Cl⁻ = 1.53 × 10⁻² from the NaCl + 2(2.00 × 10⁻²) from the CaCl₂ = 5.53 × 10⁻² mol. Ca²⁺ left = 2.00 × 10⁻² − 1.516 × 10⁻² = 4.8 × 10⁻³ mol, and the carbonate is all in the precipitate. (B) counts only one Cl⁻ per CaCl₂ (3.53 × 10⁻² mol in all) and so ranks Na⁺ first. (C) treats carbonate as the excess reactant, but Ca²⁺ was in excess. (D) assumes Ca²⁺ and CO₃²⁻ were present in exactly equal amounts, so that both are used up; in fact Ca²⁺ exceeded the carbonate by 4.8 × 10⁻³ mol.
parts.n: 4.3.A.1 and 4.5.A.2 (topic 4.3), skill 1.B. Thinking: track every ion through a precipitation: spectators stay, the excess reactant's ion stays, the limiting one leaves. Trap: (B), counting one chloride per CaCl₂.

mc.stem:
Questions 5-8 refer to the following.

A student must identify an unknown white solid that is known to be one of four weak monoprotic acids, HA.
Acid · molar mass (g/mol)
Benzoic acid · 122.12
Phenylacetic acid · 136.15
Salicylic acid · 138.12
Cinnamic acid · 148.16
In each trial she weighs a sample of the acid into a flask, dissolves it in about 25 mL of distilled water, adds 2 drops of phenolphthalein, and titrates with 0.1000 M NaOH(aq) until a pale pink color lasts for 30 seconds.
Trial · mass of acid (g) · initial buret reading (mL) · final buret reading (mL) · color at the end
1 · 0.3120 · 0.50 · 23.10 · pale pink
2 · 0.2985 · 1.20 · 24.95 · deep magenta (NaOH was added quickly near the end)
3 · 0.3050 · 0.35 · 22.43 · pale pink

parts.q:
Which acid is the unknown most likely to be, and why?
(A) Salicylic acid, because trials 1 and 3 agree at 138.1 g/mol and trial 2 went past the endpoint
(B) Phenylacetic acid, because the mean of all three trials, 134.0 g/mol, is closest to 136.15 g/mol
(C) Benzoic acid, because trial 2 used the most NaOH, so its value of 125.7 g/mol is the most complete
(D) Salicylic acid, because trial 2 used the smallest mass of acid, so its result is the least reliable
parts.a: (A). Each trial gives M = mass ÷ mol NaOH, since HA and OH⁻ react 1:1. Trial 1: 22.60 mL × 0.1000 M = 2.260 × 10⁻³ mol, so M = 0.3120 g ÷ 2.260 × 10⁻³ mol = 138.1 g/mol. Trial 3: 22.08 mL gives 2.208 × 10⁻³ mol and 138.1 g/mol. Trial 2: 23.75 mL gives 2.375 × 10⁻³ mol and 125.7 g/mol. The deep magenta color shows excess NaOH was added past the endpoint, so trial 2's volume is too large and its molar mass too low; it should be rejected. Trials 1 and 3 agree to within 0.06%, and their mean, 138.1 g/mol, matches salicylic acid (138.12) and not phenylacetic acid (136.15), which is 1.4% away. (B) averages in a trial with a known error, and the bad value drags the mean down toward 136. (C) treats extra NaOH as a more complete reaction, but NaOH added after the endpoint has no acid left to react with. (D) names the right acid for the wrong reason: the sample mass is already accounted for in the calculation; the problem with trial 2 is the overshoot.
parts.n: 4.6.A.1 (topic 4.6), skill 2.D. Thinking: compute each trial, use the lab notes to decide which trial to reject, then match the result against candidates that differ by little more than 1%. Trap: (B), averaging every trial by habit.

parts.q:
A classmate uses the same procedure on a sample of the same acid that had been left uncovered and had absorbed water from the air. He records the mass of the damp solid. How does this affect his calculated molar mass?
(A) Too low, because the water dilutes the acid, so less NaOH is needed to reach the endpoint
(B) Too low, because the water in the sample also reacts with NaOH, so more NaOH is needed
(C) Too high, because the recorded mass includes water that does not react with the NaOH
(D) Unchanged, because the sample is dissolved in water before the titration in any case
parts.a: (C). The titration counts only the moles of HA actually present, and a damp sample holds fewer moles of HA than its recorded mass suggests. The calculation divides the full recorded mass (acid + water) by those moles, so the molar mass comes out too high. (A) is right that less NaOH is needed, but fewer moles in the denominator make the quotient larger, not smaller. (B) treats water as an acid that consumes a measurable amount of NaOH; the endpoint marks the neutralization of HA, and water is the solvent in every trial. (D) confuses the water added to dissolve the sample, which changes nothing, with water weighed as if it were acid, which inflates the mass.
parts.n: 4.6.A.1 and 4.5.A.2 (topic 4.6), skill 6.G. Thinking: trace the error through M = mass ÷ moles: which quantity is wrong, and in which direction? Trap: (A), which gets 'less NaOH' right but divides the wrong way.

parts.q:
Each buret reading is uncertain by ±0.02 mL, so each titrant volume is uncertain by about ±0.04 mL. Which change to the procedure would most reduce the percent uncertainty in the titrant volume?
(A) Dissolve each sample in 100 mL of water instead of 25 mL, so that the endpoint is easier to see
(B) Use about 0.60 g of acid per trial, so that each titration needs about 43 mL of the NaOH
(C) Titrate with 0.5000 M NaOH instead of 0.1000 M, so that each trial uses less solution
(D) Use about 0.10 g of acid per trial, so that each titration needs only about 7 mL of NaOH
parts.a: (B). Percent uncertainty = ±0.04 mL ÷ volume delivered, so the larger the titrant volume, the smaller the percent uncertainty. The present trials use about 22.6 mL (0.18%). Doubling the acid to 0.60 g needs 0.60 ÷ 138.1 = 4.3 × 10⁻³ mol NaOH, or 43.4 mL, which still fits in a 50 mL buret and halves the percent uncertainty to 0.09%. (A) changes nothing about the moles of acid, so the volume of NaOH, and its uncertainty, are unchanged. (C) cuts the volume to about 4.5 mL, raising the uncertainty to about 0.9%. (D) cuts the volume to about 7.2 mL, raising it to about 0.6%.
parts.n: 4.6.A.1 (topic 4.6), skill 2.C. Thinking: a fixed reading uncertainty matters less when the measured volume is larger. Trap: (C), which confuses a quicker titration with a more precise one.

parts.q:
A student writes the net ionic equation for the titration reaction as H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), with Na⁺ and A⁻ as spectator ions. Which of the following best evaluates this equation?
(A) It is correct, because every reaction between an acid and a hydroxide has this net ionic equation.
(B) It is incorrect, because Na⁺ combines with A⁻ to form a solid salt, which must appear as a product.
(C) It is correct, because HA ionizes completely once OH⁻ is added, so H⁺ is the species that reacts.
(D) It is incorrect, because HA is a weak acid that is mostly un-ionized and donates its proton to OH⁻.
parts.a: (D). A weak acid exists in solution mostly as HA molecules, so HA itself is the proton donor: HA(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → A⁻(aq) + H₂O(l). HA and A⁻ are a conjugate acid-base pair, as are H₂O and OH⁻. A⁻ is a product of the reaction, not a spectator, and only Na⁺ is a spectator. (A) holds only for strong acids, which exist as H⁺ (H₃O⁺) and A⁻ before any base is added. (B) contradicts the solubility of sodium salts: NaA stays dissolved as Na⁺ and A⁻. (C) describes the result of the reaction as if it came first: OH⁻ removes the proton from HA in the reaction itself; HA does not first ionize fully on its own.
parts.n: 4.2.A.3 and 4.8.A.1 (topic 4.8), skill 5.E. Thinking: decide what species actually carries the proton in solution before writing the net ionic equation. Trap: (A), the strong-acid equation applied to every neutralization.

mc.stem:
Questions 9-12 refer to the following.

A student places 40.0 mL of Ba(OH)₂(aq) of unknown concentration in a beaker fitted with a conductivity probe and adds 0.0500 M H₂SO₄(aq) from a buret, recording the electrical conductivity of the mixture after each addition. A white solid, BaSO₄, forms from the first drop onward. BaSO₄ is insoluble in water; treat Ba(OH)₂ as fully dissociated into Ba²⁺ and OH⁻, and H₂SO₄ as supplying 2 H⁺ and 1 SO₄²⁻ per formula unit.
Volume of H₂SO₄ added (mL) · conductivity (µS/cm)
0.00 · 4450
2.00 · 3180
4.00 · 2020
6.00 · 970
8.00 · 12
10.00 · 1460
12.00 · 2810
A graph of conductivity against volume is two straight lines that meet at 8.00 mL.

parts.q:
What is the concentration of the Ba(OH)₂(aq)?
(A) 0.00500 M
(B) 0.00833 M
(C) 0.0100 M
(D) 0.0200 M
parts.a: (C). The conductivity reaches its minimum when the acid has exactly consumed the base: 8.00 mL × 0.0500 M = 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol H₂SO₄. The net reaction is Ba²⁺ + 2 OH⁻ + 2 H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄(s) + 2 H₂O(l), so H₂SO₄ and Ba(OH)₂ react 1:1, and 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol ÷ 0.0400 L = 0.0100 M. (A) halves the answer by counting only one H⁺ per H₂SO₄, as if two H₂SO₄ were needed for each Ba(OH)₂. (B) divides by the total volume at the equivalence point, 48.0 mL, instead of the 40.0 mL of base originally present. (D) doubles the answer by counting the 2 H⁺ per H₂SO₄ but forgetting the 2 OH⁻ per Ba(OH)₂.
parts.n: 4.6.A.1 and 4.5.A.3 (topic 4.6), skill 5.D. Thinking: read the equivalence point from where the lines meet, then use the 1:1 ratio that the charges set. Trap: (D), counting the acid's two protons but not the base's two hydroxides.

parts.q:
The student repeats the experiment with 40.0 mL of the same Ba(OH)₂(aq), but titrates it with 0.0500 M HCl(aq) instead of 0.0500 M H₂SO₄(aq). BaCl₂ is soluble in water. Which prediction about the minimum of the conductivity graph is correct?
(A) The minimum would be at 16.0 mL and well above zero, because Ba²⁺ and Cl⁻ stay dissolved.
(B) The minimum would be at 16.0 mL and near zero, because all of the OH⁻ is still converted to water.
(C) The minimum would be at 8.00 mL and well above zero, because Ba²⁺ and Cl⁻ stay dissolved.
(D) The minimum would be at 8.00 mL and near zero, because H⁺ and OH⁻ still combine to form water.
parts.a: (A). The base holds 2 × 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ = 8.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol OH⁻, and HCl supplies only one H⁺ per formula unit, so the equivalence point needs 8.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol ÷ 0.0500 M = 16.0 mL. The only net reaction is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O; no solid forms, so at the minimum the solution still holds 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol Ba²⁺ and 8.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol Cl⁻ and conducts well. (B) gets the volume right but forgets that removing OH⁻ leaves Ba²⁺ and Cl⁻ behind. (C) gets the reason right but treats HCl as supplying as many H⁺ per formula unit as H₂SO₄ does. (D) repeats the original result without accounting for either change.
parts.n: 4.2.A.3 and 4.7.A.5 (topic 4.2), skill 2.B. Thinking: write the new net ionic equation, then ask which ions it removes and which it leaves behind. Trap: (B), expecting every neutralization to drive the conductivity to zero.

parts.q:
A student claims that the conductivity falls between 0 and 8.00 mL mainly because the added acid dilutes the solution. Which of the following best evaluates this claim?
(A) The claim is supported, because conductivity depends on the concentration of ions, and each addition lowers it.
(B) The claim is not supported, because H₂SO₄ is a strong electrolyte, so adding it can only add ions to the solution.
(C) The claim is partly supported: dilution explains the fall before 8.00 mL, and the added ions explain the rise after.
(D) The claim is not supported: by 8.00 mL the volume has grown by only 20%, yet the conductivity fell by over 99%.
parts.a: (D). Dilution alone from 40.0 mL to 48.0 mL would lower the ion concentrations only to 40.0/48.0 of their values, about 17%, but the conductivity falls from 4450 to 12 µS/cm. Nearly all of the ions must be leaving the solution: Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ as solid BaSO₄, and H⁺ and OH⁻ as H₂O. The rise after 8.00 mL, while the solution keeps getting more dilute, confirms that dilution is not what controls the conductivity. (A) is true in general but cannot explain a 99% fall from a 20% volume change. (B) reaches the right verdict for the wrong reason: the added ions do not stay in solution before 8.00 mL; they are removed along with the base's ions. (C) accepts dilution as the cause of the fall, which the size of the fall rules out.
parts.n: 4.2.A.3 and 4.3.A.1 (topic 4.2), skill 6.B. Thinking: test a proposed cause against the size of the effect it would produce. Trap: (C), which sounds balanced but keeps the dilution explanation.

parts.q:
Suppose a particulate diagram of the original 40.0 mL of Ba(OH)₂(aq) shows 4 Ba²⁺ ions and 8 OH⁻ ions (water molecules not shown). Which of the following describes the diagram after 4.00 mL of the H₂SO₄(aq) has been added?
(A) 4 Ba²⁺, 4 OH⁻ and 2 SO₄²⁻ ions dissolved, and no solid
(B) 2 Ba²⁺ and 4 OH⁻ ions dissolved, and 2 formula units of solid BaSO₄
(C) 2 Ba²⁺, 4 OH⁻ and 4 H⁺ ions dissolved, and 2 formula units of solid BaSO₄
(D) 4 Ba²⁺, 8 OH⁻, 4 H⁺ and 2 SO₄²⁻ ions dissolved, and no solid
parts.a: (B). 4.00 mL is half of the 8.00 mL needed, so the acid added corresponds to 2 H₂SO₄ for the 4 Ba(OH)₂ drawn: 4 H⁺ and 2 SO₄²⁻. The 4 H⁺ combine with 4 OH⁻ to form water, and the 2 SO₄²⁻ combine with 2 Ba²⁺ to form 2 BaSO₄(s), leaving 2 Ba²⁺ and 4 OH⁻ dissolved, a neutral set. (A) treats Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ as spectators, but the stem says BaSO₄ is insoluble and forms from the first drop. (C) shows the precipitation but not the neutralization; H⁺ and OH⁻ cannot both remain, and the ions drawn carry a net +4 charge. (D) assumes nothing reacts until the equivalence point; in fact each addition reacts as it goes in.
parts.n: 4.3.A.1 and 4.5.A.2 (topic 4.3), skill 1.B. Thinking: scale the added acid to the drawn particles, apply both parts of the reaction, and check that the leftovers are neutral. Trap: (A), treating the barium and sulfate as spectator ions.

mc.stem:
Questions 13-15 refer to the following.

An older type of breath-alcohol tester bubbles a measured volume of breath through an acidified solution of potassium dichromate. Orange Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) is converted to green Cr³⁺(aq) while ethanol, C₂H₅OH, is converted to acetic acid, CH₃COOH, and the tester measures how much green Cr³⁺ forms. A student balanced the equation for acidic solution as follows.
Step 1: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14 H⁺ + 6 e⁻ → 2 Cr³⁺ + 7 H₂O
Step 2: C₂H₅OH + H₂O → CH₃COOH + 4 H⁺ + 2 e⁻
Step 3: Multiply step 2 by 3, so that both half-reactions involve 6 e⁻.
Step 4: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3 C₂H₅OH + 2 H⁺ → 2 Cr³⁺ + 3 CH₃COOH + 4 H₂O

parts.q:
In which step does the student's work first go wrong?
(A) Step 1, because each Cr changes by 3, so the half-reaction should show 3 e⁻ rather than 6 e⁻
(B) Step 2, because its charges do not balance: the left side is neutral but the right side is +2
(C) Step 3, because the half-reactions must be scaled so that the numbers of H⁺, not of e⁻, match
(D) Step 4, because the H⁺ and H₂O were cancelled wrongly, leaving the equation unbalanced for charge
parts.a: (B). Step 1 is correct: two Cr atoms each go from +6 to +3, so 6 e⁻ are gained, and the charges balance (−2 + 14 − 6 = +6 = 2 × +3). Step 2 balances C, H and O, but its right side carries 4(+1) + 2(−1) = +2 against 0 on the left; it needs 4 e⁻, since carbon's average oxidation number rises from −2 to 0 for each of the two C atoms. Steps 3 and 4 then follow correctly from the faulty step 2, which is why step 4 is atom-balanced but carries 0 on the left and +6 on the right. (A) counts the change for one Cr atom and forgets that Cr₂O₇²⁻ contains two. (C) misstates the rule: half-reactions are scaled so that electrons lost equal electrons gained. (D) points to the step where the charge imbalance first shows, but the cancelling in step 4 was done correctly; the error was inherited from step 2.
parts.n: 4.9.A.1 and 4.2.A.2 (topic 4.9), skill 5.E. Thinking: check each step for both atom and charge balance, and separate where an error starts from where it becomes visible. Trap: (D), blaming the step where the imbalance appears.

parts.q:
For one breath sample the tester finds that 6.00 × 10⁻⁵ mol of Cr³⁺ formed. Using a correctly balanced equation, what mass of ethanol (46.07 g/mol) was in the sample?
(A) 2.76 mg
(B) 3.69 mg
(C) 2.07 mg
(D) 4.15 mg
parts.a: (C). With 4 e⁻ in the ethanol half-reaction, the electrons balance at 12: 2 Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3 C₂H₅OH + 16 H⁺ → 4 Cr³⁺ + 3 CH₃COOH + 11 H₂O. So 4 mol Cr³⁺ form for every 3 mol ethanol: 6.00 × 10⁻⁵ mol × 3/4 = 4.50 × 10⁻⁵ mol ethanol, and 4.50 × 10⁻⁵ mol × 46.07 g/mol = 2.07 × 10⁻³ g = 2.07 mg. (D) uses the student's step 4 ratio of 2 Cr³⁺ to 3 ethanol, giving 9.00 × 10⁻⁵ mol and 4.15 mg. (A) assumes one ethanol per Cr³⁺. (B) inverts the correct ratio, taking 4/3 instead of 3/4 (8.00 × 10⁻⁵ mol, 3.69 mg).
parts.n: 4.9.A.1 and 4.5.A.2 (topic 4.5), skill 5.F. Thinking: rebalance by electrons, then use the product-to-reactant mole ratio. Trap: (D), trusting the student's unbalanced equation.

parts.q:
A classmate claims that the orange-to-green color change shows that the dichromate ion lost electrons. Which of the following best evaluates the claim?
(A) Incorrect, because chromium goes from +6 to +3, so it gains electrons, which come from the carbon in ethanol.
(B) Correct, because chromium goes from +6 in Cr₂O₇²⁻ to +3 in Cr³⁺, and a drop in oxidation number is a loss.
(C) Incorrect, because chromium goes from +12 to +3, so each Cr atom gains 9 electrons from the ethanol.
(D) Incorrect, because the color change comes from the H⁺ that reacts, so this is an acid-base reaction.
parts.a: (A). In Cr₂O₇²⁻, 2x + 7(−2) = −2, so each Cr is +6; in Cr³⁺ it is +3. A decrease in oxidation number means electrons were gained, and they come from carbon, whose average oxidation number rises from −2 in ethanol to 0 in acetic acid. (B) has the right oxidation numbers but the wrong direction: losing negative electrons makes an oxidation number rise, not fall. (C) forgets that the ion contains two Cr atoms and assigns the whole +12 to one of them. (D) is wrong because oxidation numbers change; H⁺ is consumed in the balanced equation, but that does not make the reaction an acid-base reaction.
parts.n: 4.7.A.3 and 4.7.A.4 (topic 4.7), skill 6.D. Thinking: assign oxidation numbers, then connect their direction of change to the direction of electron transfer. Trap: (B), which equates a drop in oxidation number with a loss of electrons.

mc.stem:
Questions 16-18 refer to the following.

A student carries out four processes and records these observations.
Process · observations
1. Solid iodine, I₂, is warmed gently in a sealed tube · purple vapor fills the tube; dark crystals form on the cool top of the tube; the total mass does not change
2. Solid ammonium chloride, NH₄Cl, is heated at the bottom of an open test tube · the white solid disappears from the hot bottom and a white solid forms near the cool mouth; the gas in the hot part of the tube contains NH₃ and HCl molecules
3. Solid ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃, is stirred into water · the solid disappears and the temperature falls from 22 °C to 9 °C; evaporating the water leaves white crystals identical to the starting solid
4. 2.470 g of pure copper(II) carbonate, CuCO₃, a green solid, is heated strongly · a colorless gas identified as CO₂ is given off; 1.590 g of a black solid remains, and its mass does not change on further heating
Molar masses (g/mol): CuCO₃ 123.56, CuO 79.55, Cu₂O 143.09, Cu 63.55

parts.q:
In processes 1 and 2 a solid disappears from a hot region and a solid forms again in a cooler region. Which of the following best explains the difference between the two processes at the particle level?
(A) In both, only the attractions between particles are overcome, because in both the same solid re-forms on cooling.
(B) In 1, the covalent I–I bonds break to give I atoms; in 2, NH₄⁺ and Cl⁻ ions leave the solid intact as gas particles.
(C) In both, chemical bonds are broken, because heating supplies energy and energy is needed to break any bond.
(D) In 1, I₂ molecules move apart intact; in 2, a proton moves from NH₄⁺ to Cl⁻, so covalent bonds break and form.
parts.a: (D). Process 1 is sublimation: the vapor is still I₂, so only the dispersion forces between molecules were overcome, a physical change. In process 2 the hot gas contains NH₃ and HCl, which are not in the solid: an N–H bond in NH₄⁺ broke and an H–Cl bond formed as the proton moved to Cl⁻, a chemical change that reverses on cooling. (A) judges by the end result only; the same solid re-forming does not show that no new substances existed in between, and the gas analysis shows they did. (B) reverses the evidence: purple I₂ vapor is molecular, and the gas in 2 is NH₃ and HCl, not ions. (C) treats all heating as bond breaking; warming iodine supplies enough energy to separate molecules, not to break I–I bonds.
parts.n: 4.4.A.1 (topic 4.4), skill 6.C. Thinking: identify which interactions change by asking what particles are present before and after, not what the change looks like. Trap: (A), classifying both by the solid that re-forms.

parts.q:
Which observation in the table is the WEAKEST evidence that a new substance formed in that process?
(A) The detection of NH₃ and HCl molecules in the hot part of the tube in process 2
(B) The colorless gas identified as CO₂ that is given off when CuCO₃ is heated in process 4
(C) The fall in temperature from 22 °C to 9 °C when NH₄NO₃ dissolves in water in process 3
(D) The black solid of constant mass that remains after CuCO₃ is heated in process 4
parts.a: (C). A temperature change is possible evidence of a chemical change, but in process 3 the table shows that evaporation returns crystals identical to the starting NH₄NO₃, so no new substance formed; the temperature fell because separating the ions from the lattice took in more energy than the ion-dipole attractions to water released. (A) is strong evidence: NH₃ and HCl are different substances from NH₄Cl. (B) is strong evidence: CO₂ was not present as a substance in the green solid. (D) is strong evidence: a new color and a new, constant mass show that a different solid remains.
parts.n: 4.1.A.1 and 4.1.A.2 (topic 4.1), skill 6.B. Thinking: weigh each observation against the other evidence recorded for the same process. Trap: (D), because a color change can occur without a reaction; here the constant new mass rules that out.

parts.q:
Which conclusion about the black solid in process 4 do the mass data best support?
(A) The black solid is Cu, formed as both CO₂ and oxygen are driven off.
(B) The black solid is CuO, formed as CO₂ is driven off.
(C) The black solid is CuO mixed with some unreacted CuCO₃.
(D) The black solid is Cu₂O, formed as CO₂ and some O₂ are driven off.
parts.a: (B). 2.470 g ÷ 123.56 g/mol = 1.999 × 10⁻² mol CuCO₃, and each formula unit keeps its one Cu atom. As CuO it would weigh 1.999 × 10⁻² mol × 79.55 g/mol = 1.590 g, exactly the mass found; the 0.880 g lost is 1.999 × 10⁻² mol of CO₂. (A) would leave 1.999 × 10⁻² mol × 63.55 g/mol = 1.270 g. (D) would leave 1.999 × 10⁻² ÷ 2 = 9.995 × 10⁻³ mol Cu₂O, or 1.430 g. (C) would weigh more than 1.590 g, and its mass would keep falling on further heating as the CuCO₃ decomposed; the table says the mass stayed constant.
parts.n: 4.5.A.1 and 4.1.A.2 (topic 4.5), skill 6.B. Thinking: conserve copper atoms, compute the mass each candidate would leave, and compare with the data. Trap: (C), which overlooks that a mass that stays constant on reheating means the decomposition was complete.

mc.stem:
Questions 19-21 refer to the following.

In one airbag design, an electrical signal heats solid sodium azide, NaN₃, which decomposes in about 30 milliseconds:
Reaction 1: 2 NaN₃(s) → 2 Na(s) + 3 N₂(g)
The sodium metal formed is dangerous, so the charge also contains excess KNO₃, which reacts with it:
Reaction 2: 10 Na(s) + 2 KNO₃(s) → K₂O(s) + 5 Na₂O(s) + N₂(g)
The bag must fill to 60.0 L at 1.10 atm and 27 °C. Use R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) and NaN₃ = 65.01 g/mol, and treat N₂ as an ideal gas.

parts.q:
Counting only the N₂ from reaction 1, what mass of NaN₃ is needed to fill the bag?
(A) 116 g
(B) 174 g
(C) 261 g
(D) 1.29 × 10³ g
parts.a: (A). n(N₂) = PV/RT = (1.10 atm)(60.0 L) ÷ [(0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K))(300. K)] = 2.68 mol. Reaction 1 gives 3 N₂ per 2 NaN₃, so n(NaN₃) = 2.68 × 2/3 = 1.79 mol, and 1.79 mol × 65.01 g/mol = 116 g. (B) uses a 1:1 ratio of NaN₃ to N₂. (C) inverts the ratio, multiplying by 3/2 instead of 2/3. (D) puts 27 in for T without converting to kelvins, which makes n(N₂) 29.8 mol.
parts.n: 4.5.A.3 (topic 4.5), skill 5.F. Thinking: go from the gas the bag needs, through PV = nRT, back to the solid through the mole ratio. Trap: (C), the inverted coefficient ratio.

parts.q:
Reaction 2 also produces N₂. If all of the Na from reaction 1 reacts in reaction 2 and that N₂ is counted too, what mass of NaN₃ is needed to fill the bag?
(A) 87.1 g
(B) 116 g
(C) 124 g
(D) 109 g
parts.a: (D). Every 2 NaN₃ give 3 N₂ directly and 2 Na; the 2 Na give 2/10 = 0.2 N₂ more in reaction 2, so 2 NaN₃ yield 3.2 N₂ in all. n(NaN₃) = 2.68 mol N₂ × 2/3.2 = 1.68 mol, and 1.68 mol × 65.01 g/mol = 109 g. (A) reads reaction 2 as 1 N₂ per 2 Na instead of per 10 Na, so 2 NaN₃ would give 4 N₂. (B) ignores the extra N₂, although it adds to the gas in the bag. (C) applies the correction in the wrong direction, multiplying the 116 g by 3.2/3 instead of dividing by it; more gas per gram of NaN₃ means less NaN₃ is needed.
parts.n: 4.5.A.1 and 4.5.A.2 (topic 4.5), skill 5.F. Thinking: combine two sequential reactions into a single mole ratio from starting material to final product. Trap: (B), counting only the obvious source of gas.

parts.q:
Which statement correctly describes the electron transfer in reaction 2?
(A) Each K atom gains 1 electron, going from +1 in KNO₃ to 0, while each Na atom loses 1 electron.
(B) Each O atom gains 2 electrons, going from 0 to −2 in the oxides, while each Na atom loses 1 electron.
(C) Each N atom gains 5 electrons, going from +5 to 0, while the 10 Na atoms lose 10 electrons in all.
(D) Each N atom loses 5 electrons, going from +5 to 0, while each Na atom gains 1 electron from nitrogen.
parts.a: (C). In KNO₃, K is +1 and each O is −2, so N is +5; in N₂ it is 0. Sodium goes from 0 in the metal to +1 in Na₂O. The 2 N atoms gain 2 × 5 = 10 electrons, exactly the 10 lost by 10 Na atoms. (A) has potassium changing, but K is +1 in both KNO₃ and K₂O. (B) forgets that oxygen is already −2 in KNO₃; it keeps that oxidation number in K₂O and Na₂O. (D) has the right oxidation numbers but the wrong direction: a drop from +5 to 0 is a gain of electrons.
parts.n: 4.7.A.2, 4.7.A.3 and 4.7.A.4 (topic 4.7), skill 1.A. Thinking: assign oxidation numbers on both sides, find which change, and check that electrons lost equal electrons gained. Trap: (B), because oxygen appears in new compounds.

parts.q:
A student tests 0.10 M solutions with a conductivity tester whose bulb glows brightly for a strong electrolyte. HCl(aq) gives a bright glow, CH₃COOH(aq) a dim glow and NH₃(aq) a dim glow. When equal volumes of the 0.10 M CH₃COOH(aq) and 0.10 M NH₃(aq) are mixed, the mixture gives a bright glow. Which of the following best explains the result for the mixture?
(A) Mixing the two solutions adds their ions together, so the mixture holds the ions of both solutions.
(B) CH₃COOH transfers a proton to NH₃, converting most of both into NH₄⁺ and CH₃COO⁻ ions.
(C) CH₃COOH and NH₃ exchange electrons, forming ions that were not present in either solution.
(D) Acetic acid ionizes completely once it is diluted by the NH₃ solution, so many H₃O⁺ ions form.
parts.a: (B). Each weak electrolyte alone is mostly molecules, which is why each glows dimly. Mixed, the acid donates protons to the base: CH₃COOH(aq) + NH₃(aq) → CH₃COO⁻(aq) + NH₄⁺(aq). This proton transfer converts most of the molecules of both into ions (ammonium salts are soluble), so the mixture is a strong electrolyte. The pairs CH₃COOH/CH₃COO⁻ and NH₄⁺/NH₃ are conjugate acid-base pairs. (A) cannot explain the result: each solution contains few ions, and mixing dilutes each by half, so simply combining them would give a glow no brighter than dim. (C) calls a proton transfer an electron transfer; no oxidation number changes (N stays −3, H stays +1). (D) is wrong because dilution does not make a weak acid ionize completely, and any H₃O⁺ would be consumed by the NH₃.
parts.n: 4.8.A.1 and 4.8.A.3 (topic 4.8), skill 6.F. Thinking: explain a change in conductivity by a reaction that creates ions, and name the proton transfer. Trap: (A), adding the ions of the two solutions together.

parts.q:
A particulate diagram shows a rigid container holding 3 C₂H₆ molecules and 7 O₂ molecules. A spark ignites the mixture, and complete combustion to CO₂ and H₂O occurs until one reactant runs out. Which of the following describes the molecules in the container after the reaction?
(A) 4 CO₂, 6 H₂O and 1 C₂H₆
(B) 6 CO₂ and 9 H₂O only
(C) 4 CO, 6 H₂O, 1 C₂H₆ and 2 O₂
(D) 4 CO₂, 6 H₂O and 1 O₂
parts.a: (A). The balanced equation is 2 C₂H₆ + 7 O₂ → 4 CO₂ + 6 H₂O. The 7 O₂ are exactly enough for 2 of the 3 C₂H₆, so O₂ is the limiting reactant: 4 CO₂ and 6 H₂O form, and 1 C₂H₆ is left over. Check: 6 C, 18 H and 14 O atoms before and after. (B) assumes both reactants are used up; it has 21 O atoms after the reaction but only 14 before. (C) conserves every atom but shows incomplete combustion to CO, and it stops while both reactants remain, which contradicts the stem. (D) makes C₂H₆ the limiting reactant; it has only 4 C atoms after the reaction but 6 before.
parts.n: 4.3.A.1 and 4.7.A.2 (topic 4.3), skill 1.A. Thinking: balance the combustion, find the limiting reactant from the particle counts, and check the result by counting atoms. Trap: (B), which uses up both reactants.

parts.q:
Student A balances the reaction of copper metal with nitric acid, which produces Cu²⁺(aq) and NO(g), as 3 Cu(s) + 2 NO₃⁻(aq) + 8 H⁺(aq) → 3 Cu²⁺(aq) + 2 NO(g) + 4 H₂O(l). Student B says the equation must be wrong: copper loses 2 electrons per atom while nitrogen gains 3, so the coefficients of Cu and NO₃⁻ ought to be equal. Which of the following best evaluates their work?
(A) B is right: electrons lost and gained can balance only if Cu and NO₃⁻ have equal coefficients.
(B) B is right, because the 8 H⁺ give the left side a charge of +8, but the right side is only +6.
(C) Both are wrong: the equation balances atoms but not charge, so the H⁺ coefficient should be 4.
(D) A is right: 3 Cu lose 6 e⁻, 2 N atoms (+5 to +2) gain 6 e⁻, and each side has a charge of +6.
parts.a: (D). Cu goes from 0 to +2 and N from +5 in NO₃⁻ to +2 in NO, so 3 Cu lose 6 electrons and 2 N gain 6. The atoms balance (3 Cu, 2 N, 6 O and 8 H on each side), and the charges are 2(−1) + 8(+1) = +6 on the left and 3(+2) = +6 on the right. (A) is student B's error: different electron counts per atom are balanced by different coefficients, as the 3:2 ratio does; equal coefficients would give 2 e⁻ lost against 3 gained. (B) forgets the two negative charges of the NO₃⁻ ions. (C) is wrong on both counts: the equation as written already balances charge (+6 on each side), and with only 4 H⁺ the left side would carry +2 against +6 and hold 4 H atoms against the 8 in 4 H₂O.
parts.n: 4.9.A.1 and 4.7.A.4 (topic 4.9), skill 6.D. Thinking: check a balanced redox equation three ways: atoms, charge and electrons. Trap: (B), which leaves the nitrate ions out of the charge count.

parts.q:
A vitamin C tablet is dissolved in water, a little starch solution is added, and the solution is titrated with 0.0250 M I₂(aq): C₆H₈O₆(aq) + I₂(aq) → C₆H₆O₆(aq) + 2 H⁺(aq) + 2 I⁻(aq). Starch forms an intense blue-black color with I₂ but not with I⁻. The first blue-black color that persists appears after 22.70 mL of I₂(aq) has been added. Which of the following gives the mass of ascorbic acid (C₆H₈O₆, 176.12 g/mol) in the tablet and describes the color during the titration?
(A) 50.0 mg; the color stays away until the end point, because each drop of I₂ is turned into I⁻ while any C₆H₈O₆ remains
(B) 99.9 mg; the color appears with the first drop of I₂ and grows steadily darker until the equivalence point
(C) 99.9 mg; the color stays away until the end point, because each drop of I₂ is turned into I⁻ while any C₆H₈O₆ remains
(D) 200. mg; the color appears only at the end point, because only then has enough I⁻ built up to color the starch
parts.a: (C). n(I₂) = 0.02270 L × 0.0250 M = 5.675 × 10⁻⁴ mol, which reacts 1:1 with ascorbic acid: 5.675 × 10⁻⁴ mol × 176.12 g/mol = 0.0999 g = 99.9 mg. Before the equivalence point, each drop of I₂ is consumed at once, so only I⁻ is present and the starch stays colorless; the first excess I₂ turns it blue-black, which is why the color marks the end point. (A) has the right description but halves the mass by reading the 2 I⁻ (or 2 H⁺) as a 2:1 ratio of I₂ to ascorbic acid. (B) has the right mass but would make the color useless as an indicator: I₂ does not accumulate while ascorbic acid remains. (D) doubles the mass by inverting that misread ratio, taking 2 mol ascorbic acid per I₂, and credits I⁻, which the stem says does not color starch.
parts.n: 4.6.A.1 and 4.5.A.3 (topic 4.6), skill 5.F. Thinking: link the indicator's behavior to which species is in excess, and use the titrant-to-analyte ratio from the equation. Trap: (B), expecting the color to build up gradually.

fr.title: Identifying a carbonate by mass loss
fr.stem:
A student is given 1.000 g of a white solid known to be one of four carbonates.
Carbonate · molar mass (g/mol)
MgCO₃ · 84.31
CaCO₃ · 100.09
SrCO₃ · 147.63
BaCO₃ · 197.34
She pipets 50.00 mL of 0.500 M HCl(aq), enough to be in excess for any of the four, into a flask and weighs it. She adds the 1.000 g of solid, swirls the flask until no more bubbles form, and weighs it again. All four chlorides are soluble in water.
Measurement · mass (g)
Flask + 50.00 mL of HCl(aq), before the solid is added · 151.614
Flask + contents, after the 1.000 g of solid is added and the bubbling stops · 152.316
Afterward she titrates the solution left in the flask with 0.400 M NaOH(aq) to a phenolphthalein endpoint, to find how much HCl was left over. Use CO₂ = 44.01 g/mol.

parts.q: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the reaction of the solid carbonate, represented as MCO₃(s), with HCl(aq).
parts.a: MCO₃(s) + 2 H⁺(aq) → M²⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). The solid is written as a formula unit because it is insoluble; Cl⁻ is a spectator ion. Check: one M, one C, three O and two H on each side, and a charge of +2 on each side.
parts.n: CO₃²⁻(aq) + 2 H⁺(aq) → H₂O + CO₂ earns nothing: it shows the solid as dissolved ions. MCO₃ + 2 HCl → MCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂ is a molecular equation, not a net ionic one.

parts.q: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ released.
parts.a: 6.77 × 10⁻³ mol. The mass before reaction is 151.614 + 1.000 = 152.614 g, and the mass lost is the CO₂ that escaped: 152.614 − 152.316 = 0.298 g. Then 0.298 g ÷ 44.01 g/mol = 6.77 × 10⁻³ mol CO₂.
parts.n: Subtracting 152.316 from 151.614 without adding the solid earns nothing; dividing the mass of the solid by 44.01 earns nothing, since only the mass lost is CO₂.

parts.q: Determine the molar mass of the carbonate, identify it, and justify your identification.
parts.a: SrCO₃. By the 1:1 ratio of MCO₃ to CO₂ in part (a), n(MCO₃) = 6.77 × 10⁻³ mol, so the molar mass is 1.000 g ÷ 6.77 × 10⁻³ mol = 148 g/mol (1 point). That matches SrCO₃ (147.63 g/mol) and is far from CaCO₃ (100.09) and BaCO₃ (197.34); equivalently, 1.000 g of SrCO₃ would release 0.298 g of CO₂, exactly the mass lost (1 point).
parts.n: A molar mass with no comparison to the table earns only the first point. Choosing the carbonate from the mass of solid alone, or from the volume of HCl, earns nothing.

parts.q: A classmate claims that if the student had used 100.00 mL of the 0.500 M HCl instead of 50.00 mL, twice as much mass would have been lost. Do you agree? Justify your answer.
parts.a: Disagree. The 50.00 mL already holds 2.50 × 10⁻² mol HCl, and the carbonate needs only 2 × 6.77 × 10⁻³ = 1.35 × 10⁻² mol. The carbonate is the limiting reactant, so it fixes the amount of CO₂ at 6.77 × 10⁻³ mol (0.298 g); more acid only adds to the excess.
parts.n: Agreeing because 'more reactant makes more product' earns nothing. 'Disagree, the HCl is in excess' without a comparison of moles does not earn the point.

parts.q: If the identification in part (c) is correct, calculate the volume of 0.400 M NaOH(aq) needed to titrate the HCl left in the flask.
parts.a: 28.6 mL. HCl at the start: 0.05000 L × 0.500 M = 2.50 × 10⁻² mol; HCl used by the carbonate: 2 × 6.77 × 10⁻³ = 1.354 × 10⁻² mol; HCl left: 2.50 × 10⁻² − 1.354 × 10⁻² = 1.146 × 10⁻² mol (1 point). H⁺ and OH⁻ react 1:1, so V = 1.146 × 10⁻² mol ÷ 0.400 M = 0.0286 L = 28.6 mL (1 point).
parts.n: Using a 1:1 ratio of HCl to carbonate (which gives 45.6 mL) loses the first point. Titrating all 2.50 × 10⁻² mol of HCl (62.5 mL) earns nothing: part of the acid has already reacted.

parts.q: Some of the CO₂ produced stays dissolved in the solution when the final mass is recorded. Predict whether the calculated molar mass of the carbonate would be too high, too low or unaffected. Justify your prediction.
parts.a: Too high (1 point). CO₂ that stays in the flask is still weighed, so the mass lost is smaller than the CO₂ actually produced. The calculated moles of CO₂, and therefore of MCO₃, are too small, and 1.000 g divided by too few moles gives too large a molar mass (1 point).
parts.n: 'Too high' with no chain from mass lost to moles to molar mass earns only the first point. 'Too low, because less CO₂ was produced' earns nothing: the same amount of CO₂ was produced, only less of it escaped.

parts.q: The teacher says that even if 0.010 g of CO₂ remained dissolved, the identification in part (c) would not change. Justify or refute the teacher's statement with a calculation.
parts.a: The teacher is right. With 0.010 g more CO₂, the true loss would be 0.308 g, or 0.308 ÷ 44.01 = 7.00 × 10⁻³ mol, giving 1.000 g ÷ 7.00 × 10⁻³ mol = 143 g/mol. That is still far closer to SrCO₃ (147.63) than to CaCO₃ (100.09) or BaCO₃ (197.34), so the identification stands.
parts.n: Subtracting the 0.010 g instead of adding it (0.288 g, 153 g/mol) reaches the right verdict from the wrong correction and earns nothing. A verdict with no calculation earns nothing.

fr.title: Hypochlorite in bleach by iodine titration
fr.stem:
Household bleach contains the hypochlorite ion, OCl⁻. A student adds a 2.00 mL sample of bleach (density 1.08 g/mL) to a flask containing excess KI(aq) and acid. Reaction 1 goes to completion:
Reaction 1: OCl⁻(aq) + 2 I⁻(aq) + 2 H⁺(aq) → Cl⁻(aq) + I₂(aq) + H₂O(l)
The I₂ formed is then titrated with 0.1000 M Na₂S₂O₃(aq), and 34.60 mL is needed to reach the endpoint:
Reaction 2: I₂(aq) + 2 S₂O₃²⁻(aq) → 2 I⁻(aq) + S₄O₆²⁻(aq)
Use NaOCl = 74.44 g/mol. I₂ is slightly volatile: it slowly escapes from an open flask as a vapor.

parts.q: Using oxidation numbers, identify the element that is oxidized and the element that is reduced in reaction 1. Justify your answer.
parts.a: Iodine is oxidized and chlorine is reduced. I goes from −1 in I⁻ to 0 in I₂, a loss of electrons. Cl goes from +1 in OCl⁻ (since O is −2 and the ion is −1) to −1 in Cl⁻, a gain of 2 electrons per Cl, matching the 2 electrons lost by the 2 I⁻.
parts.n: Naming the species without oxidation numbers earns nothing. Calling oxygen or hydrogen the element reduced earns nothing: O stays −2 and H stays +1.

parts.q: Calculate the percent by mass of NaOCl in the bleach.
parts.n: Skipping the 2:1 ratio in reaction 2 doubles the answer (11.9%) and earns nothing; dividing by 2.00 g instead of the sample's mass (6.44%) also earns nothing.

parts.q: A student claims that using twice as much KI would make the calculated percent of NaOCl too high, because more I₂ would form. Do you agree? Justify your answer.
parts.a: Disagree. KI is already in excess, so OCl⁻ is the limiting reactant in reaction 1. The amount of I₂ formed is set by the OCl⁻: one I₂ per OCl⁻. Extra I⁻ has no OCl⁻ left to react with, so the same I₂ forms, the same volume of thiosulfate is needed, and the result is unaffected.
parts.n: Agreeing earns nothing. 'Disagree, KI is a spectator' earns nothing: I⁻ is a reactant, just an excess one.

parts.q: Before titrating, the student leaves the flask open on the bench for 20 minutes. Predict whether the calculated percent of NaOCl will be too high, too low or unaffected. Justify your prediction.
parts.a: Too low. Some of the I₂ formed in reaction 1 escapes as vapor, so less I₂ remains to be titrated and less thiosulfate is needed. The calculation converts that smaller volume back into fewer moles of OCl⁻, so the calculated percent is too low.
parts.n: 'Too high, because the solution gets more concentrated as it stands' earns nothing: the moles of I₂, not its concentration, set the volume of titrant. A prediction with no justification earns nothing.

fr.title: Three unlabeled solutions
fr.stem: Three unlabeled bottles contain 0.5 M NaCl(aq), 0.5 M HCl(aq) and 0.5 M Na₂CO₃(aq), one solution in each. A student may mix small samples of the solutions with one another in test tubes, and she has one strip of magnesium ribbon, which she may cut into pieces. She has no other reagents or indicators. All sodium salts are soluble in water.

parts.q: The student mixes a sample of each solution with a sample of each of the other two. Predict what she will observe for each of the three pairs, and explain how the results identify the NaCl(aq).
parts.a: HCl + Na₂CO₃: bubbles of gas (CO₂). NaCl + HCl and NaCl + Na₂CO₃: no visible change, since no new substance forms (all the possible products are soluble and no gas or water forms). The bottle whose solution gives no change with either of the other two is NaCl; the two that bubble together are HCl and Na₂CO₃.
parts.n: Predicting a precipitate for any pair earns nothing. Identifying NaCl without saying which pairs bubble earns nothing.

parts.q: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the reaction that produces a gas when two of the solutions are mixed, and identify the Brønsted-Lowry acid and base in it.
parts.a: 2 H⁺(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). H⁺ (present in water as H₃O⁺) is the Brønsted-Lowry acid, since it donates protons, and CO₃²⁻ is the base, since it accepts them; Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectators.
parts.n: 2 HCl + Na₂CO₃ → 2 NaCl + H₂O + CO₂ is a molecular equation and earns nothing; naming Na₂CO₃ (rather than CO₃²⁻) as the base does not earn the point.

parts.q: Describe how the student can use the magnesium ribbon to tell the HCl(aq) from the Na₂CO₃(aq). Predict what she will see, and justify the prediction.
parts.a: Drop a piece of magnesium into a sample of each. It fizzes steadily in HCl(aq), because Mg(s) + 2 H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g): the acid supplies H⁺ ions that take electrons from Mg. In Na₂CO₃(aq) there is essentially no H⁺, so no steady fizzing is seen. The bottle in which Mg fizzes is HCl; the other is Na₂CO₃.
parts.n: A procedure with no predicted observation, or a prediction with no reason, earns nothing. Predicting CO₂ from Mg + HCl earns nothing: the gas is H₂.

parts.q: A classmate claims that the gas-forming reactions in parts (b) and (c) are both oxidation-reduction reactions, because each produces a gas. Evaluate the claim using oxidation numbers.
parts.a: The claim is only half right. Mg + 2 H⁺ is a redox reaction: Mg goes from 0 to +2 and H from +1 to 0. The carbonate reaction is not: C is +4 in both CO₃²⁻ and CO₂, O stays −2 and H stays +1, so no electrons are transferred; it is an acid-base reaction (proton transfer). Forming a gas does not by itself show electron transfer.
parts.n: Agreeing with the claim earns nothing. Rejecting it for both reactions, or classifying them without oxidation numbers, earns nothing.

u5.intro: A periodic table and the AP Chemistry equations sheet are allowed, and a calculator may be used throughout.

mc.stem:
Questions 1-3 refer to the following.

A student studies the reaction S₂O₈²⁻(aq) + 2 I⁻(aq) → 2 SO₄²⁻(aq) + I₂(aq) at 22 °C. Each reaction mixture also contains starch and 1.0 × 10⁻³ M S₂O₃²⁻(aq), which instantly turns any I₂ formed back into I⁻: I₂ + 2 S₂O₃²⁻ → 2 I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻. Once all of the S₂O₃²⁻ is used up, I₂ builds up and the starch suddenly turns blue-black. The student records the time for the blue-black color to appear. The total volume is the same in every trial.
Trial · [I⁻]₀ (M) · [S₂O₈²⁻]₀ (M) · time for blue-black color (s)
1 · 0.080 · 0.040 · 44
2 · 0.040 · 0.040 · 87
3 · 0.080 · 0.020 · 89
4 · 0.120 · 0.040 · 30

parts.q:
Which rate law is consistent with the data?
(A) rate = k[I⁻]²[S₂O₈²⁻]
(B) rate = k[I⁻][S₂O₈²⁻]
(C) rate = k[I⁻]⁻¹[S₂O₈²⁻]⁻¹
(D) rate = k[I⁻]²[S₂O₈²⁻]²
parts.a: (B). Every trial forms the same amount of I₂ before the color appears, so the rate is inversely proportional to the time. Halving [I⁻] (trial 1 to 2) doubles the time (44 s to 87 s), so it halves the rate: first order in I⁻. Trial 4 confirms it: 1.5 times the [I⁻] cuts the time by a factor of 1.5 (44 s to 30 s). Halving [S₂O₈²⁻] (trial 1 to 3) also doubles the time: first order in S₂O₈²⁻. (A) takes the order of I⁻ from its coefficient in the equation; a second-order dependence would cut the time in trial 4 to 44 ÷ 2.25 = 20 s. (C) treats the time as if it were the rate. (D) reads 'the time doubled' as 'second order', without asking what doubling the time does to the rate.
parts.n: 5.2.A.2, 5.2.A.3 and 5.2.A.5 (topic 5.2), skill 5.C. Thinking: convert a clock time into a rate before comparing trials. Trap: (A), the order read from the balanced equation.

parts.q:
The student plans a fifth trial at 22 °C with [I⁻]₀ = 0.060 M and [S₂O₈²⁻]₀ = 0.030 M, keeping 1.0 × 10⁻³ M S₂O₃²⁻. About how long should the blue-black color take to appear?
(A) 25 s
(B) 59 s
(C) 78 s
(D) 104 s
parts.a: (C). The rate is proportional to [I⁻][S₂O₈²⁻]. Compared with trial 1, that product is (0.060 × 0.030) ÷ (0.080 × 0.040) = 0.5625 times as large, so the rate is 0.5625 times as fast, and the same amount of I₂ takes 44 s ÷ 0.5625 = 78 s to form. (A) multiplies the time by 0.5625, as though a slower reaction took less time. (B) applies only one of the two factors of 3/4. (D) treats the reaction as second order in I⁻, dividing by (0.75)² × 0.75.
parts.n: 5.2.A.2 (topic 5.2), skill 5.F. Thinking: scale the rate by the rate law, then turn the rate back into a time. Trap: (A), which scales the time the same way as the rate.

parts.q:
Suppose the student had used 2.0 × 10⁻³ M S₂O₃²⁻ in every trial instead of 1.0 × 10⁻³ M but still calculated each rate as 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ M of I₂ divided by the time. How would this affect the orders and the value of k that she determines?
(A) The orders and k would both be unaffected, because the rate law of the reaction does not change.
(B) Both orders would appear to be 2, and k would be unaffected, because every time doubles.
(C) The orders would be unaffected, and k would be twice the true value, because more S₂O₃²⁻ reacts.
(D) The orders would be unaffected, and k would be half the true value, because every time doubles.
parts.a: (D). With twice the S₂O₃²⁻, twice as much I₂ (1.0 × 10⁻³ M) must form before the color appears, so every time doubles while the true rates are unchanged. Orders come from ratios of rates between trials, and doubling every time leaves every ratio the same, so the orders are unaffected. But each calculated rate, 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ M ÷ (doubled time), is half the true rate, so k comes out half its true value. (A) is right that the reaction's rate law does not change, but the student's calculated rates do. (B) confuses a change common to every trial with a change in how the rate depends on concentration. (C) gets the direction wrong: longer times make the calculated rates, and so k, smaller.
parts.n: 5.2.A.4 and 5.2.A.5 (topic 5.2), skill 6.G. Thinking: separate what depends on ratios between trials (orders) from what depends on the absolute rate (k). Trap: (A), because 'the reaction is the same'.

mc.stem:
Questions 4-7 refer to the following.

A pharmaceutical chemist stores a solution of a drug, D, at 40 °C and measures its concentration every 10 days. The decomposition has only one reactant: D → products.
Time (days) · [D] (mM) · ln[D] · 1/[D] (mM⁻¹)
0 · 5.00 · 1.609 · 0.200
10 · 4.10 · 1.411 · 0.244
20 · 3.37 · 1.215 · 0.297
30 · 2.76 · 1.015 · 0.362
40 · 2.26 · 0.815 · 0.442

parts.q:
Which of the following gives the order of the reaction with respect to D and the rate constant?
(A) First order, k = 0.0199 day⁻¹
(B) Zero order, k = 0.0685 mM day⁻¹
(C) Second order, k = 0.00606 mM⁻¹ day⁻¹
(D) First order, k = 0.198 day⁻¹
parts.a: (A). ln[D] falls by the same amount, about 0.198 to 0.200, in every 10-day interval, so a plot of ln[D] against time is linear and the reaction is first order. The slope is (0.815 − 1.609) ÷ 40 days = −0.0199 day⁻¹, so k = 0.0199 day⁻¹. (B) takes the average slope of [D] against time, but [D] falls by 0.90, 0.74, 0.60 and 0.50 mM in successive intervals, so that plot curves. (C) takes the average slope of 1/[D], but its steps grow from 0.044 to 0.080 mM⁻¹, so that plot curves too. (D) has the right order but divides the drop in ln[D] by one interval instead of by 10 days.
parts.n: 5.3.A.1, 5.3.A.2 and 5.3.A.4 (topic 5.3), skill 5.D. Thinking: test each transformed column for constant differences over equal times, then take the slope with its time units. Trap: (D), the drop per interval read as a drop per day.

parts.q:
The drug is considered unusable once 10% of it has decomposed. About how long does that take at 40 °C?
(A) 3.5 days
(B) 7.0 days
(C) 5.3 days
(D) 116 days
parts.a: (C). For a first-order reaction, ln([D]₀/[D]) = kt. When 10% has decomposed, [D]/[D]₀ = 0.90, so t = ln(1/0.90) ÷ 0.0199 day⁻¹ = 0.105 ÷ 0.0199 = 5.3 days. (A) takes 10% of the half-life (0.10 × 34.8 days), as if the amount lost were proportional to the fraction of a half-life. (B) takes one-fifth of the half-life, reasoning that 10% is one-fifth of 50%; first-order losses are not linear in time. (D) finds the time for the drug to fall to 10% remaining, ln(10) ÷ k, which is when 90% has decomposed.
parts.n: 5.3.A.4 and 5.3.A.5 (topic 5.3), skill 5.F. Thinking: turn 'fraction decomposed' into [D]/[D]₀ and use the integrated first-order law instead of scaling the half-life. Trap: (B), treating a first-order loss as linear.

parts.q:
A colleague claims that a solution made at twice the concentration, 10.0 mM, will stay usable (less than 10% decomposed) for twice as long at 40 °C. Which of the following best evaluates the claim?
(A) It is correct, because there is twice as much drug to decompose, and the rate constant is unchanged.
(B) It is incorrect: doubling [D] doubles the rate too, so the time to lose 10% of the drug is unchanged.
(C) It is incorrect: doubling [D] makes the rate four times as fast, so the time to lose 10% is halved.
(D) It is correct, because the half-life of a first-order reaction is proportional to the initial [D].
parts.a: (B). For a first-order reaction the rate is k[D], so twice the concentration decomposes twice as fast, and the time to lose a given fraction, ln(1/0.90) ÷ k, depends only on k. The 10.0 mM solution also takes 5.3 days to lose 10%. The data show this too: the fraction lost in each 10-day interval stays at about 18% while [D] falls. (A) assumes the rate stays the same when [D] doubles, which would be zero-order behavior. (C) treats the reaction as second order. (D) states the opposite of the first-order result: t½ = 0.693/k does not depend on [D]₀.
parts.n: 5.3.A.5 (topic 5.3), skill 6.D. Thinking: for first order, the time to lose a fixed fraction depends on k alone. Trap: (A), which keeps the rate fixed when the concentration doubles.

parts.q:
The chemist suspects that H⁺ from an acidic additive in the formulation speeds up the decomposition. Which experiment would best test this?
(A) Measure k at several temperatures between 30 °C and 50 °C, using the formulation with the additive.
(B) Measure k at 40 °C for solutions with [D]₀ = 2.50, 5.00 and 10.0 mM, all made with the additive.
(C) Measure [D] after 60 days at 40 °C in the formulation with the additive, to see whether it is below 2.50 mM.
(D) Measure k at 40 °C for solutions of the same [D]₀ made at several fixed [H⁺], with no other change.
parts.a: (D). To test whether H⁺ affects the rate, [H⁺] must be the only variable: the same drug, the same [D]₀ and the same temperature, with several fixed [H⁺] values. If k rises with [H⁺], H⁺ speeds up the reaction (acid catalysis). (A) varies temperature, which changes k whether or not H⁺ plays a part. (B) varies [D]₀, which for a first-order reaction leaves k unchanged and says nothing about H⁺. (C) adds one more measurement under a single set of conditions and has nothing to compare it with.
parts.n: 5.1.A.3 and 5.11.A.4 (topic 5.1), skill 2.C. Thinking: isolate one variable and hold the rest fixed. Trap: (A), because temperature is the variable most often changed in kinetics experiments.

mc.stem:
Questions 8-10 refer to the following.

Chloroform reacts with chlorine: CHCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g) → CCl₄(g) + HCl(g). A student measures initial rates at one temperature.
Trial · [CHCl₃]₀ (M) · [Cl₂]₀ (M) · initial rate (M/s)
1 · 0.010 · 0.010 · 1.5 × 10⁻⁵
2 · 0.020 · 0.010 · 3.0 × 10⁻⁵
3 · 0.010 · 0.040 · 3.0 × 10⁻⁵
Three mechanisms are proposed.
Mechanism 1: a single step, CHCl₃ + Cl₂ → CCl₄ + HCl
Mechanism 2: Step 1 (fast, reversible): Cl₂ ⇌ 2 Cl; Step 2 (slow): Cl + CHCl₃ → HCl + CCl₃; Step 3 (fast): CCl₃ + Cl → CCl₄
Mechanism 3: Step 1 (slow): Cl₂ → 2 Cl; Step 2 (fast): Cl + CHCl₃ → HCl + CCl₃; Step 3 (fast): CCl₃ + Cl → CCl₄

parts.q:
Which rate law is consistent with the data?
(A) rate = k[CHCl₃][Cl₂]^½
(B) rate = k[CHCl₃][Cl₂]
(C) rate = k[CHCl₃]²[Cl₂]^½
(D) rate = k[CHCl₃][Cl₂]²
parts.a: (A). From trial 1 to trial 2, [CHCl₃] doubles with [Cl₂] fixed and the rate doubles: first order in CHCl₃. From trial 1 to trial 3, [Cl₂] is multiplied by 4 and the rate only doubles: 4ˣ = 2, so x = ½. (B) takes the orders from the coefficients of the overall equation, which would make the rate four times as fast in trial 3. (C) squares [CHCl₃], which would make the rate four times as fast in trial 2. (D) inverts the Cl₂ comparison, reading 'the concentration is the square of the rate factor' as 'the rate is the square of the concentration factor'.
parts.n: 5.2.A.3 and 5.2.A.5 (topic 5.2), skill 5.C. Thinking: an order need not be a whole number; solve (concentration factor)ˣ = rate factor. Trap: (D), which sets up the ratio the wrong way round.

parts.q:
Which of the proposed mechanisms is consistent with the experimental rate law?
(A) Mechanism 1 only, since it is the only one in which both reactants collide
(B) Mechanism 3 only, since its slow step is the one that breaks the Cl–Cl bond
(C) Mechanism 2 only, since its fast equilibrium makes [Cl] vary as [Cl₂]^½
(D) Mechanisms 2 and 3, since both make the Cl atoms that react with CHCl₃
parts.a: (C). Mechanism 2's slow step gives rate = k₂[Cl][CHCl₃]. Step 1 is a fast equilibrium, so K = [Cl]²/[Cl₂] and [Cl] = (K[Cl₂])^½; substituting gives rate = k₂K^½[CHCl₃][Cl₂]^½, which matches. (A) is wrong because a single elementary step CHCl₃ + Cl₂ would give rate = k[CHCl₃][Cl₂], first order in Cl₂. (B) is wrong because a slow first step Cl₂ → 2 Cl gives rate = k[Cl₂]: first order in Cl₂ and zero order in CHCl₃. (D) includes mechanism 3, which has the same steps as mechanism 2 but a different slow step, and so a different rate law.
parts.n: 5.9.A.1 and 5.8.A.1 (topic 5.9), skill 5.B. Thinking: write each mechanism's rate law from its slow step, using a fast equilibrium to replace an intermediate. Trap: (D), judging mechanisms by their steps instead of by their slow step.

parts.q:
A student objects that mechanism 2 cannot be correct, because its slow step contains Cl atoms, which do not appear in the overall equation, so its rate law would have to contain [Cl]. Which of the following best evaluates the objection?
(A) It is valid: a rate law is written from the slow step exactly as it stands, so [Cl] has to appear in it.
(B) It fails: the fast equilibrium in step 1 ties [Cl] to [Cl₂], so [Cl] can be rewritten in terms of [Cl₂].
(C) It fails, because Cl is a catalyst, and a catalyst never appears in the rate law of a reaction.
(D) It is valid, because an intermediate can never be a reactant in the rate-limiting step of a mechanism.
parts.a: (B). Cl is an intermediate, made in step 1 and used up in steps 2 and 3. A rate law written from the slow step may contain an intermediate at first, but because step 1 is a fast equilibrium, [Cl] = (K[Cl₂])^½ can be substituted, leaving only species in the overall equation: rate = k[CHCl₃][Cl₂]^½. (A) stops before that substitution; an experimental rate law can contain only species whose concentrations are measured. (C) mislabels Cl: a catalyst is present at the start and regenerated, while Cl is made and then consumed. (D) is false: intermediates are often reactants in the slow step, which is exactly when a pre-equilibrium is needed.
parts.n: 5.9.A.1 and 5.7.A.3 (topic 5.9), skill 6.D. Thinking: an intermediate in the slow step is eliminated through the fast equilibrium that forms it. Trap: (A), which stops at a rate law containing [Cl].

mc.stem:
Questions 11-13 refer to the following.

The figure, described here in words, shows the distribution of molecular kinetic energies in the same gas-phase reaction mixture at two temperatures. The horizontal axis is the kinetic energy of a molecule; the vertical axis is the fraction of molecules with that energy. Curve X (300 K) rises from the origin to a tall, narrow peak and then falls toward zero. Curve Y (310 K) has a lower, broader peak at a slightly higher energy and a longer tail at high energy.
Two vertical lines are drawn. Line 1, at the activation energy E₁ of reaction 1, lies far out in the tail of both curves; the area under curve Y to the right of line 1 is about 2 times the area under curve X to the right of it. Line 2, at a higher energy E₂, is the activation energy of reaction 2; the area under curve Y to the right of line 2 is about 4 times the area under curve X to the right of it.
Measurements show that the rate constant of reaction 1 at 310 K is about twice its value at 300 K, while kinetic theory predicts that the number of collisions per second rises by only about 2% between these two temperatures.

parts.q:
A student claims that the rate constant of reaction 1 doubles mainly because the molecules collide twice as often at 310 K. Which of the following best evaluates the claim?
(A) Incorrect: collisions are only about 2% more frequent; the doubling comes from twice the fraction reaching E₁.
(B) Correct, because the rate of an elementary reaction is proportional to the number of collisions per second.
(C) Incorrect: the activation energy is lower at 310 K, so collisions with less energy are now able to react.
(D) Incorrect: at 310 K a larger fraction of the collisions have the correct orientation, which doubles the rate.
parts.a: (A). A 2% rise in collision frequency cannot double the rate. What doubles is the fraction of collisions energetic enough to reach the transition state: the area beyond line 1 under curve Y is about twice that under curve X, matching the doubled rate constant. (B) states a true proportionality but ignores the 2% figure in the data. (C) is wrong because the activation energy is a property of the reaction pathway; line 1 is at the same energy for both curves. (D) is wrong because the fraction of collisions with a suitable orientation depends on the shapes of the molecules, not on the temperature, and nothing in the figure concerns orientation.
parts.n: 5.5.A.2, 5.5.A.3 and 5.6.A.4 (topic 5.5), skill 6.E. Thinking: compare the size of each proposed cause with the size of the effect. Trap: (B), a true statement that cannot account for the numbers.

parts.q:
Reactions 1 and 2 have similar collision frequencies and orientation requirements. Which prediction about reaction 2 does the figure support?
(A) Its rate constant also about doubles from 300 K to 310 K, because both reactions are warmed by the same 10 K.
(B) Its rate constant rises by a smaller factor than reaction 1's, because fewer molecules have energies beyond E₂.
(C) Its rate constant rises by a larger factor, about 4, as the fraction beyond E₂ about quadruples.
(D) Its rate constant is larger than reaction 1's at both temperatures, because its fraction beyond E₂ grows faster.
parts.a: (C). With collision frequency and orientation similar, each rate constant scales with the fraction of molecules beyond that reaction's activation energy. Beyond E₂ that fraction grows about fourfold from 300 K to 310 K, against about twofold beyond E₁, so reaction 2's rate constant rises by the larger factor: the higher the barrier, the more sensitive the rate is to temperature. (A) assumes the same temperature change has the same effect on every reaction, but the figure shows different ratios. (B) confuses the size of a fraction with how fast it grows: fewer molecules lie beyond E₂, but that small fraction grows proportionally more. (D) reverses the absolute comparison: at each temperature the area beyond E₂ is smaller than the area beyond E₁, so reaction 2 is the slower reaction.
parts.n: 5.6.A.4 and 5.5.A.3 (topic 5.6), skill 5.D. Thinking: read a ratio of two areas, not their sizes, to judge how strongly a rate depends on temperature. Trap: (B), mixing up 'smaller fraction' with 'smaller increase'.

parts.q:
Suppose half of the gas is pumped out of the container while the temperature is held at 300 K. A student claims that curve X would then be half as tall at every energy, and that this is why reaction 1 becomes slower. Which of the following best evaluates the claim?
(A) Correct: with half as many molecules, the area under the whole curve and the area beyond line 1 are both halved.
(B) Incorrect: the curve shifts to lower energies, because fewer molecules are left to share the kinetic energy.
(C) Incorrect: the curve is unchanged, and so is the rate of reaction 1, because the temperature is still 300 K.
(D) Incorrect: the curve is unchanged, as it shows fractions; the rate falls because collisions are less frequent.
parts.a: (D). The vertical axis is the fraction of molecules at each energy, and at a fixed temperature that distribution does not depend on how many molecules there are: curve X keeps its shape and height, and the fraction of collisions with at least E₁ is unchanged. Reaction 1 slows because there are fewer molecules per unit volume, so collisions of every kind happen less often; the rate constant is unchanged, but the rate falls. (A) reads the vertical axis as a number of molecules rather than a fraction; the area under a fraction curve stands for the whole sample, whatever its size. (B) ties the energy of each molecule to how many molecules there are, but the distribution of kinetic energies is set by the temperature alone. (C) has the curve right but confuses the rate constant, which depends on temperature, with the rate, which also depends on how often the molecules collide.
parts.n: 5.5.A.1 and 5.5.A.3 (topic 5.5), skill 4.D. Thinking: separate what the energy distribution shows (the fraction of molecules at each energy, set by temperature) from what sets the collision frequency (the number of molecules per unit volume). Trap: (A), reading a fraction-of-molecules axis as a number of molecules.

mc.stem:
Questions 14-16 refer to the following.

An enzyme, E, catalyzes the conversion of a substrate, S, into a product, P. A proposed mechanism is:
Step 1 (fast, reversible): E + S ⇌ ES
Step 2 (slow): ES → E + P
A biochemist measures the initial rate of formation of P at several substrate concentrations, using the same total concentration of enzyme in every trial.
[S] (mM) · initial rate (µM/s)
0.20 · 0.91
0.50 · 2.0
1.0 · 3.3
2.0 · 5.0
5.0 · 7.1
10.0 · 8.3
20.0 · 9.1

parts.q:
Which statement about the order of the reaction with respect to S is best supported by the data?
(A) It is first order over the whole range, because the rate rises every time [S] is increased.
(B) It is close to first order at low [S] and approaches zero order at high [S].
(C) It is close to zero order at low [S] and approaches first order at high [S].
(D) It is half order throughout, because doubling [S] raises the rate by about 1.4 times.
parts.a: (B). At low [S] the rate nearly keeps pace with [S]: from 0.20 to 0.50 mM (2.5 times), the rate rises 2.2 times. At high [S] it hardly changes: doubling [S] from 10.0 to 20.0 mM raises the rate only from 8.3 to 9.1 µM/s, about 1.1 times, so the order approaches zero. (A) confuses 'the rate increases' with 'the rate is proportional'; first order would double the rate for every doubling of [S]. (C) reverses the trend in the data. (D) fits only the middle of the table, where doubling [S] from 1.0 to 2.0 mM raises the rate about 1.5 times; the factor for a doubling falls from about 1.7 (0.50 to 1.0 mM) to about 1.1 (10.0 to 20.0 mM), so no single order fits.
parts.n: 5.2.A.2 and 5.11.A.3 (topic 5.11), skill 5.D. Thinking: compare the rate factor with the concentration factor in different ranges of the data. Trap: (A), reading any increase as first order.

parts.q:
A student claims that the rate levels off at high [S] because the enzyme is used up by the reaction. Which of the following best evaluates the claim?
(A) Correct, because each enzyme molecule reacts with one S molecule in step 1 and is then consumed.
(B) Correct, because ES is an intermediate that builds up and cannot react any further once it forms.
(C) Incorrect: at high [S] the many S molecules get in one another's way, so fewer of them reach E.
(D) Incorrect: E is regenerated in step 2, but at high [S] nearly all of it is bound as ES.
parts.a: (D). E is a catalyst: it is used in step 1 and returned in step 2, so none is used up. The rate is set by the slow step, rate = k[ES]. At high [S] almost all of the enzyme is tied up as ES at any moment, so [ES] cannot rise further and the rate levels off at k times the total enzyme concentration. (A) reads step 1 without step 2. (B) is wrong because ES does react further, in step 2; it is its breakdown that limits the rate. (C) invents crowding that is not part of the mechanism; the mechanism explains the plateau by the limited number of enzyme molecules.
parts.n: 5.7.A.1, 5.11.A.2 and 5.11.A.3 (topic 5.7), skill 6.D. Thinking: tell a catalyst that is tied up from one that is used up, and connect the slow step to the plateau. Trap: (A), which forgets that step 2 releases E.

parts.q:
The experiment is repeated with twice the total concentration of enzyme and the same values of [S]. Which prediction is best supported by the mechanism?
(A) The rate doubles at every [S], because twice as many enzyme molecules are available to form ES.
(B) The rate is unchanged at every [S], because a catalyst is not consumed by the reaction.
(C) Only the rates at high [S] double; at low [S] the rate depends only on how much S is present.
(D) Only the rates at low [S] double; at high [S] the rate is already at its maximum and cannot rise.
parts.a: (A). The rate is k[ES]. At any [S], the same fraction of the enzyme is bound as ES, so doubling the total enzyme doubles [ES] and the rate. At high [S] the plateau, k times the total enzyme concentration, also doubles. (B) confuses not being consumed with having no effect; more catalyst means more ES. (C) forgets that at low [S] the rate also depends on how much E is there to bind S. (D) treats the plateau as a fixed ceiling, but its height is set by the amount of enzyme.
parts.n: 5.11.A.3 and 5.8.A.1 (topic 5.11), skill 2.B. Thinking: trace the effect of the catalyst's concentration through the slow step at both ends of the data. Trap: (D), a plateau read as a property of the reaction alone.

mc.stem:
Questions 17-19 refer to the following.

A student drops 2.50 g of marble chips, CaCO₃ (100.09 g/mol), into 50.0 mL of 2.00 M HCl(aq) in a flask on a balance. A loose cotton plug in the neck lets gas escape but stops spray. The reaction is CaCO₃(s) + 2 H⁺(aq) → Ca²⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g), and the mass lost equals the mass of CO₂ that has escaped. Assume the volume of solution stays 50.0 mL. Use CO₂ = 44.01 g/mol.
Time (s) · total mass lost (g)
0 · 0.00
20 · 0.38
40 · 0.64
60 · 0.82
90 · 0.98
120 · 1.06
180 · 1.10
240 · 1.10

parts.q:
What is the average rate of consumption of H⁺(aq), in M/s, between 20 s and 40 s?
(A) 5.91 × 10⁻³ M/s
(B) 1.18 × 10⁻² M/s
(C) 1.45 × 10⁻² M/s
(D) 2.91 × 10⁻² M/s
parts.a: (B). Between 20 s and 40 s, 0.64 − 0.38 = 0.26 g of CO₂ escaped: 0.26 g ÷ 44.01 g/mol = 5.91 × 10⁻³ mol. Two H⁺ are used per CO₂, so 1.18 × 10⁻² mol H⁺ was consumed from 0.0500 L, a drop of 0.236 M in 20 s, or 1.18 × 10⁻² M/s. (A) is the rate of CO₂ production expressed per liter; it leaves out the 2:1 ratio. (C) averages over the whole first 40 s instead of the interval asked for. (D) divides the total mass lost at 40 s, instead of the change since 20 s, by 20 s.
parts.n: 5.1.A.1 and 5.1.A.2 (topic 5.1), skill 5.F. Thinking: take a change over the interval, convert it to moles, and scale by the coefficients to the species asked about. Trap: (A), which skips the 2:1 ratio.

parts.q:
The student repeats the experiment with the same 2.50 g of marble chips but with 50.0 mL of 0.800 M HCl(aq) in place of the 2.00 M acid. Which prediction is correct?
(A) The initial rate would be lower, and the final mass lost would still be 1.10 g, because the CaCO₃ is unchanged.
(B) The initial rate would be the same, because the chips are unchanged, and the final mass lost would be 0.880 g.
(C) The initial rate would be the same, because the chips are unchanged, and the final mass lost would be 1.10 g.
(D) The initial rate would be lower, because [H⁺] is lower, and the final mass lost would be 0.880 g.
parts.a: (D). A lower [H⁺] means fewer collisions of H⁺ with the CaCO₃ surface per second, so the initial rate is lower. The amount of product changes too: 0.0500 L × 0.800 M = 0.0400 mol HCl, but 2.50 g of CaCO₃ (2.50 × 10⁻² mol) needs 5.00 × 10⁻² mol HCl, so HCl is now the limiting reactant. It gives 0.0400 ÷ 2 = 0.0200 mol CO₂, or 0.0200 × 44.01 = 0.880 g. (A) keeps CaCO₃ as the limiting reactant, which is what a 1:1 ratio of HCl to CaCO₃ would suggest; with the 2:1 ratio the acid runs out first. (B) gets the yield right but ignores the effect of concentration on rate. (C) misses both changes.
parts.n: 5.1.A.3 and 5.5.A.1 (topic 5.1), skill 2.B. Thinking: separate what controls how fast (collisions of H⁺ with the surface) from what controls how much (the limiting reactant), and recheck which reactant limits. Trap: (A), which assumes the solid always limits the yield.

parts.q:
The student wants to test how the concentration of HCl affects the rate of this reaction. Which pair of trials is a fair test?
(A) 2.50 g of chips of one size, with 50.0 mL of 1.50 M HCl and with 50.0 mL of 2.00 M HCl, both at 22 °C
(B) 2.50 g of chips with 50.0 mL of 2.00 M HCl, and 2.50 g of powder with 50.0 mL of 1.50 M HCl, both at 22 °C
(C) 2.50 g of chips with 50.0 mL of 2.00 M HCl at 22 °C, and 2.50 g of chips with 50.0 mL of 1.50 M HCl at 32 °C
(D) 2.50 g of chips with 50.0 mL of 2.00 M HCl, and 5.00 g of chips with 50.0 mL of 1.50 M HCl, both at 22 °C
parts.a: (A). Only the HCl concentration differs; the mass and size of the chips, the volume of acid and the temperature are all the same, and both acids are in excess (0.0750 mol and 0.100 mol of HCl against the 0.0500 mol needed), so any difference in rate can be credited to concentration. (B) changes the surface area at the same time as the concentration, and the two effects work in opposite directions. (C) changes the temperature as well. (D) doubles the mass of chips, and so the surface area in contact with the acid, as well.
parts.n: 5.1.A.3 (topic 5.1), skill 2.C. Thinking: a fair test changes one variable and controls every other factor that affects rate. Trap: (C), where the temperature change is easy to overlook.

mc.stem:
Questions 20-21 refer to the following.

Nitryl chloride decomposes at high temperature: 2 NO₂Cl(g) → 2 NO₂(g) + Cl₂(g). In three experiments at the same temperature, the initial concentration of NO₂Cl was 0.020 M, 0.040 M and 0.080 M, and in each experiment the concentration of NO₂Cl fell to half its initial value in 38 s.

parts.q:
A student claims that the reaction occurs in a single elementary step in which two NO₂Cl molecules collide. Which of the following best evaluates the claim?
(A) Correct, because the balanced equation shows two NO₂Cl molecules as the reactants.
(B) Incorrect: that step would be second order, so its half-life would double each time [NO₂Cl]₀ was halved.
(C) Incorrect: an elementary step must be unimolecular, and this equation has two reactant molecules.
(D) Correct, because a constant half-life shows that every collision of two NO₂Cl molecules leads to reaction.
parts.a: (B). A bimolecular elementary step 2 NO₂Cl → products would have rate = k[NO₂Cl]², and a second-order half-life, t½ = 1/(k[NO₂Cl]₀), that doubles each time the starting concentration is halved. The half-life is 38 s at all three starting concentrations, which is the mark of a first-order reaction, so the claimed single step is ruled out. (A) takes the rate law from the coefficients of an equation that is not shown to be elementary. (C) overstates the rule: bimolecular elementary steps are common; it is steps with three or more particles that are rare. (D) invents a meaning for a constant half-life; it tells the order, not the fraction of collisions that succeed.
parts.n: 5.4.A.1 and 5.3.A.5 (topic 5.4), skill 6.D. Thinking: predict how a proposed elementary step would behave, then check it against the half-life data. Trap: (A), the rate law read off the balanced equation.

parts.q:
Which proposed mechanism is consistent with the data?
(A) Step 1 (slow): NO₂Cl + NO₂Cl → NO₂ + NO₂Cl₂; Step 2 (fast): NO₂Cl₂ → NO₂ + Cl₂
(B) Step 1 (fast, reversible): NO₂Cl ⇌ NO₂ + Cl; Step 2 (slow): NO₂Cl + Cl → NO₂ + Cl₂
(C) Step 1 (slow): NO₂Cl → NO₂ + Cl; Step 2 (fast): NO₂Cl + Cl → NO₂ + Cl₂
(D) Step 1 (fast, reversible, twice): NO₂Cl ⇌ NO₂ + Cl; Step 2 (slow): Cl + Cl → Cl₂
parts.a: (C). Its slow first step is unimolecular, so rate = k[NO₂Cl], first order, as the constant half-life requires; the second NO₂Cl is consumed in the fast step after it, and the steps add up to the overall equation.
